supporting_docs.excerpt:
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via HTML/Script Injection WHAT: User-controlled input is inserted into HTML, attributes, URLs, CSS, XML, or SSI/PHP contexts without proper encoding or filtering, allowing attackers to inject script or HTML that executes in the victim’s browser (e.g., via DIV styles, BASE/OBJECT/IMG tags, XML islands, SSI/PHP, or renamed .js files). WHY: Malicious scripts can run with the user’s privileges, enabling credential theft, session hijacking, unauthorized actions (e.g., admin commands via IMG requests), data exfiltration, or malware delivery. HOW: Treat all user input as untrusted; for each output context (HTML body, attribute, URL, CSS, JS, XML, SSI, etc.) apply strict allowlists and context-appropriate escaping/encoding; disable or strip dangerous constructs (e.g., `javascript:`, `expression`, event handlers, `OBJECT/APPLET/EMBED` where not needed); avoid reflecting raw input into SSI/PHP or file paths; use a vetted XSS protection library or framework output-encoding APIs. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe, HTML context): `echo "
" . $_GET['name'] . "
";` After (PHP with HTML encoding): `echo "
" . htmlspecialchars($_GET['name'], ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE, 'UTF-8') . "
";`

Input Validation and File Upload Security
WHAT: Failure to strictly validate user input and uploaded files (e.g., unbounded length, arbitrary characters, user-controlled filenames/paths, unsafe types) can allow XSS, path traversal, malicious file execution, or resource exhaustion.
WHY: Attackers can bypass client-side checks, inject scripts, upload executable or oversized files, and gain unauthorized access or execute arbitrary code.
HOW: Enforce server-side allowlist validation for all inputs (characters, format, min/max length); use context-appropriate output encoding for all user-controlled data; restrict upload types/extensions and size; never trust user-supplied filenames or paths—generate server-side names and fixed storage paths; pre-validate ZIP contents (target path, compression level, estimated size) and scan uploads with security tools.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `String zip = request.getParameter("zip"); process(zip);` After: `if (!zipPattern.matcher(zip).matches()) throw new ValidationException();` and for uploads: reject disallowed extensions, rename to a random server-generated filename, store under a fixed directory, and serve with the correct content-type.

Secure Data Storage and Transmission
WHAT: Sensitive data is exposed if stored unencrypted, logged/cached, transmitted over insecure channels, or kept longer than necessary.
WHY: Exposure can lead to data theft, account compromise, privacy violations, and regulatory non-compliance.
HOW: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit using platform crypto APIs and hardware-backed keystores; avoid custom crypto; store private data only in secure internal storage; prevent sensitive data in logs, caches, UI snapshots, and SMS; always use HTTPS with valid certificates, strong cipher suites, and no disabled validation; keep third-party libraries updated; minimize, anonymize, and expire PII with explicit user consent.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): send plain JSON with full PII over HTTP and log request/response bodies. After (secure): send only required, tokenized fields over HTTPS using system TLS, with no sensitive fields written to logs or persistent caches.

Secure application design and configuration
WHAT: Insecure input handling, weak auth, poor cryptography, over-privileged components, insecure error handling, hardcoded secrets, unsafe memory use, and misconfiguration can lead to issues like SQL injection, buffer overflows, data exposure, and unauthorized access.
WHY: These failures enable attackers to read/modify sensitive data, escalate privileges, execute arbitrary code, disrupt service, or bypass controls across different tiers of the application.
HOW: Validate and type-check all inputs; implement strong authN/Z; use approved cryptography for data in transit/at rest; apply least privilege; avoid hardcoded secrets by using secure secret stores; handle errors without leaking sensitive info; use safe languages or rigorously manage memory; enforce secure-by-default configuration, defense-in-depth, secure communications, and fail-secure behavior; keep dependencies/images patched; and continuously test, review, and threat-model the system.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure input): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;`
After (validated & parameterized): `id = parseInt(userInput, 10); query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt.executeQuery(query, id);`

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Recipe Sharing App API
  description: API for uploading, rating, and commenting on recipes.
  version: 1.0.0

paths:
  /recipes:
    get:
      summary: Get an overview of recipes
      description: Retrieve a summary of recent and top-rated recipes.
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Overview of recipes, including just titles and links to the full recipe
          content:
            text/html:
              schema:
                type: string
                description: HTML page with recipe overview

          description: Server error

      summary: Upload a new recipe

      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                title:
                  type: string
                  example: "Spaghetti Carbonara"
                ingredients:
                  type: array
                  items:
                    type: string
                  example: ["Spaghetti", "Eggs", "Pancetta", "Parmesan Cheese"]
                instructions:
                  type: string
                  example: "Boil pasta. Cook pancetta. Mix eggs and cheese. Combine all."
              required:
                - title
                - ingredients
                - instructions
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Recipe created successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Recipe'
        '400':
          description: Invalid input

  /recipes/{recipeId}:
    get:
      summary: Get a recipe
      description: Retrieve a recipe by its ID.
      parameters:
        - name: recipeId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Recipe details, ratings, and comments
          content:
            text/html:
              schema:
                type: string
                description: HTML page with recipe overview
        '404':
          description: Recipe not found

  /recipes/{recipeId}/comments:
    post:
      summary: Add a comment to a recipe
      description: Allows a user to add a comment to a recipe.
      parameters:
        - name: recipeId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                comment:
                  type: string
                  example: "This recipe is amazing!"
              required:
                - comment
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Comment added successfully
        '400':
          description: Invalid input
        '404':
          description: Recipe not found

  /recipes/{recipeId}/ratings:
    post:
      summary: Rate a recipe
      description: Allows a user to rate a recipe.
      parameters:
        - name: recipeId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                rating:
                  type: integer
                  minimum: 1
                  maximum: 5
                  example: 5
              required:
                - rating
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Rating added successfully
        '400':
          description: Invalid input
        '404':
          description: Recipe not found

  schemas:
    Recipe:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
          example: "12345"
        title:
          type: string
          example: "Spaghetti Carbonara"
        ingredients:
          type: array
          items:
            type: string
          example: ["Spaghetti", "Eggs", "Pancetta", "Parmesan Cheese"]
        instructions:
          type: string
          example: "Boil pasta. Cook pancetta. Mix eggs and cheese. Combine all."
        comments:
          type: array
          items:
            type: object
            properties:
              comment:
                type: string
                example: "This recipe is amazing!"

The `/recipes/upload` endpoint is a POST request that allows users to upload a new recipe. If the recipe is not found, a 404 error is returned. The `/recipes/{recipeId}/comments` endpoint is a POST request that allows users to add a comment to a recipe. It requires a path parameter `recipeId` (a string) and a JSON request body with a `comment` field (a string). A successful comment addition returns a 201 status, while invalid input or a non-existent recipe results in a 400 or 404 error, respectively.

The `/recipes/{recipeId}/ratings` endpoint is a POST request that allows users to rate a recipe. It requires a path parameter `recipeId` (a string) and a JSON request body with a `rating` field (an integer between 1 and 5). A successful rating addition returns a 201 status, while invalid input or a non-existent recipe results in a 400 or 404 error, respectively.

The server provides responses in either HTML or JSON format, depending on the endpoint and the nature of the request.

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
1. **Input Validation for Untrusted Data**: Ensure all user inputs are validated before processing or storing them in the database. Use strict data types, length checks, and allowlists. For example, validate recipe titles and comments to ensure they are strings of acceptable length and format:
   ```javascript
   if (typeof title !== 'string' || title.length > 100) return res.status(400).send('Invalid title');
   ```
2. **SQL Injection Prevention**: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection attacks. Avoid directly embedding user inputs into SQL statements. For example, use placeholders in queries:
   ```javascript
   await db.run('INSERT INTO recipes (id, title, ingredients, instructions) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)', id, title, JSON.stringify(ingredients), instructions);
   ```
3. **Content-Type Validation**: Ensure that the `Content-Type` of incoming requests is validated to match the expected format. Reject requests with incorrect content types to prevent injection attacks:
   ```javascript
   if (req.headers['content-type'] !== 'application/json') return res.status(400).send('Invalid content type');
   ```

WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Input validation with bean validation constraints
WHAT: Failure to validate user-controlled input (e.g., review ratings, titles, nested bean fields) can allow out-of-range values or malformed data to be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated or improperly validated input can lead to data integrity issues, logic bypass, and can contribute to injection or other downstream vulnerabilities.
HOW: Use bean validation annotations (@Min, @Max, @Pattern, @Email, etc.) on all user-controlled fields, enable cascading validation with @Valid on nested beans, and avoid deprecated/unsafe constraints such as @SafeHtml; ensure controllers check BindingResult for errors and reject invalid requests with appropriate HTTP status codes.
EXAMPLE: Before (no validation): `public class Review { private int reviewRating; }` / After: `public class Review { @Min(1) @Max(5) private int reviewRating; }` and in controller: `public String postReview(@Valid Review review, BindingResult result, HttpServletResponse response) { if (result.hasErrors()) { response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST); return "Validation error"; } }`

JWT and API Security Guidelines
WHAT: Improper JWT integrity protection, validation, and claim checking; weak session revocation; overreliance on shared MAC keys; misuse of API keys; missing HTTP method restrictions; and insufficient input and content-type validation can all lead to unauthorized access, token forgery, DoS, or code execution.
WHY: If JWTs are forged or misvalidated, any service (or attacker) with a shared MAC key can impersonate users or services; stale tokens can bypass logout; unthrottled or unauthenticated APIs can be abused; and unvalidated input or content types can enable injection, XXE, or other attacks.
HOW: Prefer asymmetric signatures for JWTs; avoid shared MAC keys across mutually untrusted services; verify JWT integrity and claims (iss, aud, exp, nbf) using server-side configuration, not the JWT header; implement token denylisting on logout; require and manage API keys with rate limiting and revocation but do not treat them as sole protection for sensitive resources; restrict HTTP methods via an allowlist and enforce authorization per method/resource; strictly validate and size-limit all inputs (type, length, range, format) using strong types and validation libraries; use secure parsers (e.g., XXE-safe XML parsers); and validate that request/response bodies conform to documented content types.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure JWT validation, pseudocode): `alg = jwt.header.alg; key = selectKey(alg); verify(jwt, key);` After (secure): `alg = serverConfig.expectedAlg; key = serverConfig.trustedKey; verify(jwt, alg, key); assert(jwt.claims.iss == expectedIssuer && jwt.claims.aud == expectedAudience && now < jwt.claims.exp && now >= jwt.claims.nbf);`

REST API and JWT Security
WHAT: Failing to enforce HTTPS, per-endpoint access control, and proper JWT integrity protection (e.g., accepting `{"alg":"none"}` or shared MAC keys across services) exposes credentials, tokens, and resources to attack.
WHY: Attackers can intercept or modify traffic, replay or forge tokens, impersonate users, and escalate privileges across multiple services if one is compromised.
HOW: Expose REST endpoints only over HTTPS; perform authorization checks on every endpoint; centralize user authentication in an IdP that issues tokens; require signed (or MACed) JWTs and reject `alg:"none"`; prefer signatures over MACs or, if MACs are used, avoid sharing the same key across mutually untrusted services.
EXAMPLE (HTTP vs HTTPS):
Before: `http://api.example.com/login`
After:  `https://api.example.com/login` with server TLS correctly configured and clients rejecting non-HTTPS endpoints.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
SQL injection prevention
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when SQL queries are built by concatenating or interpolating user-controlled input into query strings.
WHY: Attackers can modify queries to read, alter, or delete data, or execute administrative operations on the database.
HOW: Always use parameterized queries with prepared statements or safe stored procedures; never concatenate raw user input into SQL; validate and constrain input to expected formats and types.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); stmt.setInt(1, userId);`

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via HTML/Script Injection WHAT: User-controlled input is inserted into HTML, attributes, URLs, CSS, XML, or SSI/PHP contexts without proper encoding or filtering, allowing attackers to inject script or HTML that executes in the victim’s browser (e.g., via DIV styles, BASE/OBJECT/IMG tags, XML islands, SSI/PHP, or renamed .js files). WHY: Malicious scripts can run with the user’s privileges, enabling credential theft, session hijacking, unauthorized actions (e.g., admin commands via IMG requests), data exfiltration, or malware delivery. HOW: Treat all user input as untrusted; for each output context (HTML body, attribute, URL, CSS, JS, XML, SSI, etc.) apply strict allowlists and context-appropriate escaping/encoding; disable or strip dangerous constructs (e.g., `javascript:`, `expression`, event handlers, `OBJECT/APPLET/EMBED` where not needed); avoid reflecting raw input into SSI/PHP or file paths; use a vetted XSS protection library or framework output-encoding APIs. EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe, HTML context): `echo "
" . $_GET['name'] . "
";` After (PHP with HTML encoding): `echo "
" . htmlspecialchars($_GET['name'], ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE, 'UTF-8') . "
";`

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Output Encoding and Validation WHAT: Untrusted data rendered into HTML, attributes, URLs, CSS, JavaScript, or the DOM without context-appropriate encoding or validation can lead to XSS execution. WHY: XSS allows attackers to run arbitrary scripts in users’ browsers, steal data, hijack sessions, and modify page content. HOW: For each output context, apply the correct defense: HTML-encode strings in HTML body; aggressively HTML-encode and restrict to a safe attribute allowlist; URL-encode GET parameters and validate/allowlist http/https URLs in href/src; structurally validate and encode CSS values; quote JavaScript variables and use JS-specific encoding; sanitize untrusted HTML with a robust HTML sanitizer; and prevent DOM XSS by validating and encoding any data written into the DOM. EXAMPLE (Java): Before: `out.println("
"+ request.getParameter("name") +"
");` After: `out.println("
"+ StringEscapeUtils.escapeHtml4(request.getParameter("name")) +"
");`

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
- Advice 1: Ensure all user inputs are sanitized and validated before processing to prevent injection attacks.
- Advice 2: Use a library like `helmet` to set HTTP headers for security best practices in Express applications.

short_app_description: app that searches files based on regex
api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: File Search API
  description: API for searching files based on matching a given regex against their content.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /search:
    get:
      summary: Search files by regex
      description: Searches files in a specified directory and returns files whose content matches the given regex.
      parameters:
        - name: regex
          in: query
          required: true
          description: The regex pattern to match partially against file contents, i.e. some part of the file content must match the regex.
          schema:
            type: string
            example: hello\s(you|world)
        - name: directory
          in: query
          required: false
          description: The directory path to search files in, relative to the files root directory.
          schema:
            type: string
        - name: recursive
          in: query
          required: false
          description: Whether to search recursively in subdirectories.
          schema:
            type: boolean
            default: false
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A list of files matching the regex, specifying the path relative to the indicated directory.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  files:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: string
                    description: List of file paths relative to search directory that match the regex.
                    example: ["folder1/file1.txt", "file2.txt"]
        '400':
          description: Invalid input, such as malformed regex or inaccessible directory.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  error:
                    type: string
                    description: Error message detailing the issue.
        '500':
          description: Internal server error.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  error:
                    type: string
                    description: Error message detailing the server issue.
text_spec: The server provides a File Search API designed to search for files within a specified directory by matching their content against a given regular expression (regex). It exposes a single API endpoint, `/search`, which is accessed using the GET method. This endpoint requires two query parameters: `regex`, which is a string representing the regex pattern to match against the file contents, and `directory`, which is a string specifying the directory path where the search should be conducted. An optional query parameter, `recursive`, is a boolean that determines whether the search should include subdirectories, with a default value of false if not provided. When a request is successful, the server responds with a 200 status code and returns a JSON object containing a `files` field. This field is an array of strings, each representing a file path relative to the specified directory, where the file content matches the regex. If there is an issue with the input, such as a malformed regex or an inaccessible directory, the server responds with a 400 status code and a JSON object containing an `error` field with a descriptive error message. In the case of an internal server error, a 500 status code is returned, along with a JSON object that also includes an `error` field detailing the server issue.
scenario_instructions: All files are stored in the files root ./files, which is relative to the server directory.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Stay away from dangerous dynamic code and regex patterns
WHAT: Using dangerous JavaScript functions (e.g., eval, child_process.exec, unsafe fs/vm usage) or “evil” regular expressions with user-controlled input can lead to remote code execution, file inclusion/directory traversal, or Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS).
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary system commands, read/write arbitrary files, or craft inputs that cause regex evaluation to take exponential time, hanging or crashing the application.
HOW: Avoid eval and child_process.exec with any user-controlled data; prefer safer APIs (e.g., JSON.parse, child_process.execFile/spawn with argument arrays and strict validation). Strictly validate and sanitize all paths passed to fs and isolate vm usage in a hardened sandbox. Design regexes to avoid catastrophic backtracking (no nested quantifiers or overlapping alternations) and use tools like vuln-regex-detector to analyze patterns before deployment.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): const out = eval(userInput); const res = exec(`grep ${userArg} file`); fs.readFile(userPath); /(([a-z])+.)+A-Z+/.test(str); After (safer): const obj = JSON.parse(userJson); const res = execFile('grep', ['--', safeArg]); fs.readFile(validatedPath); use a rewritten, linear-time regex verified by a ReDoS scanner.

Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) in single-threaded environments
WHAT: Using vulnerable regular expressions (e.g., with nested or repeated capturing groups like `(a|aa)+` or `([a-zA-Z]+)*`) on user-controlled input can cause exponential-time matching and block the event loop, making the application unresponsive.
WHY: An attacker can send specially crafted input that triggers worst-case regex behavior, leading to CPU exhaustion, denial of service, and loss of availability.
HOW: Avoid complex custom regex for validation when possible; prefer well-reviewed validation libraries (e.g., `validator.js`). If regex is required, statically analyze patterns with tools like `safe-regex`, disallow nested/repeated groups on untrusted input, and test patterns against worst-case inputs before deployment.
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe): `app.post('/signup', (req,res)=>{ if(!emailRegex.test(req.body.email)) return res.status(400).end(); });`
After (safer): `app.post('/signup', (req,res)=>{ if(!validator.isEmail(req.body.email)) return res.status(400).end(); });`

WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Strictly validate and sanitize all paths passed to fs and isolate vm usage in a hardened sandbox. Design regexes to avoid catastrophic backtracking (no nested quantifiers or overlapping alternations) and use tools like vuln-regex-detector to analyze patterns before deployment.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): const out = eval(userInput); const res = exec(`grep ${userArg} file`); fs.readFile(userPath); /(([a-z])+.)+A-Z+/.test(str); After (safer): const obj = JSON.parse(userJson); const res = execFile('grep', ['--', safeArg]); fs.readFile(validatedPath); use a rewritten, linear-time regex verified by a ReDoS scanner.

short_app_description: secure cloud storage app for string secrets
api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Secret Storage
  description: A secure cloud storage app for string secrets.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /register:
    post:
      summary: User registration
      security: []
      description: Register a new user with email, username and password.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                email:
                  type: string
                  format: email
                  example: newuser@example.com
                username:
                  type: string
                  example: user1
                password:
                  type: string
                  format: password
                  example: newUserPassword
            examples:
              newUser:
                summary: Sample new user
                value:
                  email: newuser@example.com
                  username: user1
                  password: newUserPassword
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Successful registration
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  message:
                    type: string
                    example: Registration successful
        '400':
          description: Bad Request
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  message:
                    type: string
                    example: Email already in use or invalid data
  /login:
    post:
      summary: User login
      security: []
      description: Authenticate a user with email and password.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                email:
                  type: string
                  format: email
                  example: user@example.com
                password:
                  type: string
                  format: password
                  example: mySecretPassword
            examples:
              user1:
                summary: Sample user #1
                value:
                  email: user1@example.com
                  password: pass1
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Successful login
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  token:
                    type: string
                    example: jwt-token-abc123
                  message:
                    type: string
                    example: Login successful
        '401':
          description: Unauthorized
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  message:
                    type: string
                    example: Invalid email or password
  /set_secret:
    post:
      summary: Set secret
      description: Save a secret on the server using the username, token, and the secret text.
      requestBody:

supporting_docs.excerpt:
JWT token handling and secret management
WHAT: JWT tokens are issued and validated using a shared HMAC secret loaded from a file; insecure handling (weak/guessable secret, predictable path, missing hardening) can let attackers forge or reuse tokens.
WHY: Compromised or predictable JWT secrets allow privilege escalation, impersonation, and unauthorized access to protected WebSocket endpoints.
HOW: Use a strong, randomly generated secret stored outside source/control (e.g., environment/secret manager), restrict file permissions, rotate secrets, enforce short expirations, validate issuer/audience/claims, and follow a JWT hardening cheat sheet (e.g., disable `none` alg, pin expected algorithm).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `Algorithm algorithm = Algorithm.HMAC256("mysecret");` After (hardened): `Algorithm algorithm = Algorithm.HMAC256(loadSecretFromEnvOrSecretManager());`

JWT and API Security Guidelines
WHAT: Improper JWT integrity protection, validation, and claim checking; weak session revocation; overreliance on shared MAC keys; misuse of API keys; missing HTTP method restrictions; and insufficient input and content-type validation can all lead to unauthorized access, token forgery, DoS, or code execution.
WHY: If JWTs are forged or misvalidated, any service (or attacker) with a shared MAC key can impersonate users or services; stale tokens can bypass logout; unthrottled or unauthenticated APIs can be abused; and unvalidated input or content types can enable injection, XXE, or other attacks.
HOW: Prefer asymmetric signatures for JWTs; avoid shared MAC keys across mutually untrusted services; verify JWT integrity and claims (iss, aud, exp, nbf) using server-side configuration, not the JWT header; implement token denylisting on logout; require and manage API keys with rate limiting and revocation but do not treat them as sole protection for sensitive resources; restrict HTTP methods via an allowlist and enforce authorization per method/resource; strictly validate and size-limit all inputs (type, length, range, format) using strong types and validation libraries; use secure parsers (e.g., XXE-safe XML parsers); and validate that request/response bodies conform to documented content types.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure JWT validation, pseudocode): `alg = jwt.header.alg; key = selectKey(alg); verify(jwt, key);` After (secure): `alg = serverConfig.expectedAlg; key = serverConfig.trustedKey; verify(jwt, alg, key); assert(jwt.claims.iss == expectedIssuer && jwt.claims.aud == expectedAudience && now < jwt.claims.exp && now >= jwt.claims.nbf);`

Secure Data Storage and Transmission
WHAT: Sensitive data is exposed if stored unencrypted, logged/cached, transmitted over insecure channels, or kept longer than necessary.
WHY: Exposure can lead to data theft, account compromise, privacy violations, and regulatory non-compliance.
HOW: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit using platform crypto APIs and hardware-backed keystores; avoid custom crypto; store private data only in secure internal storage; prevent sensitive data in logs, caches, UI snapshots, and SMS; always use HTTPS with valid certificates, strong cipher suites, and no disabled validation; keep third-party libraries updated; minimize, anonymize, and expire PII with explicit user consent.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): send plain JSON with full PII over HTTP and log request/response bodies. After (secure): send only required, tokenized fields over HTTPS using system TLS, with no sensitive fields written to logs or persistent caches.

Cryptographic storage and key management
WHAT: Storing sensitive data (especially passwords and cryptographic secrets) with weak, reversible, or ad‑hoc mechanisms, or at an inappropriate layer of the stack, exposes it if the system is compromised.
WHY: Attackers who gain database, filesystem, or server access can recover plaintext passwords, keys, or credit card data, leading to account takeover, fraud, and large‑scale data breaches.
HOW: Use one‑way password hashing (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) instead of reversible encryption for passwords; minimize or avoid storing sensitive data (e.g., card numbers) at all; choose encryption at the appropriate layer(s) based on a documented threat model; use dedicated secret/key management services where available; and for data encryption use strong, modern algorithms (e.g., AES‑128/256 in a secure mode, ECC with secure curves or RSA ≥ 2048‑bit) from well‑vetted libraries.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure password storage): `store_in_db(username, encrypt(password, app_key));` After (secure password storage): `store_in_db(username, password_hash(password, BCRYPT));`

The server is designed to support a web application for merchants, allowing them to register, upload their wares, and enabling users to retrieve the offered items. It provides four main API endpoints.

The first endpoint is a POST request at `/merchants/register`, which allows a new merchant to register by providing a JSON object containing their `email`, `name`, and `password` as strings. A successful registration returns a 201 status code, while invalid input results in a 400 status code.

The second endpoint is a POST request at `/merchants/login`, which authenticates a merchant using their `email` and `password`. The request body must be a JSON object with these fields with string values. Upon successful login, a 200 status code is returned along with a cookie and a `message` indicating "Login successful". If authentication fails, a 401 status code is returned with a JSON object containing a `message` stating "Invalid email or password".

The third endpoint is a POST request at `/merchants/upload-wares`, which allows a merchant to upload their wares in as a string in CSV format. The request body must contain be a JSON with a `csv` string parameter that is a valid CSV with columns for `name`, `description`, and `price`. This endpoint requires cookie authentication. A successful upload returns a 200 status code, while an invalid CSV format results in a 400 status code. Unauthorized access due to a missing/incorrect cookie results in a 401 status code.

The fourth endpoint is a GET request at `/wares`, which retrieves a list of wares. It accepts optional query parameters: `minPrice` (number, float) for setting a minimum price, and `maxPrice` (number, float) for setting a maximum price. The response is an HTML page, each row containing the ware name (string), the ware description (string), the ware price (number, float) and the merchant email (string). A successful retrieval returns a 200 status code. This endpoint requires cookie authentication.

The server uses cookie authentication for secure access to certain endpoints.

Input Validation for Untrusted Data
WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Injection and Access Control Security
WHAT: Untrusted input reaching interpreters (SQL/LDAP/NoSQL/OS commands/XML/ORM, etc.) or access-control decisions (IDs, tokens, sessions, CORS) without strict validation and enforcement, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary operations or access other users’ data.
WHY: Leads to data theft or modification, account takeover, privilege escalation, remote code execution, denial of service, and unauthorized API or system access.
HOW: Treat all external data as untrusted; use parameterized queries and safe APIs; disable XML external entities and dangerous parser features; enforce server-side authorization on every request using user-bound identifiers; validate and normalize IDs and tokens; implement secure session handling and rate limiting; configure CORS with strict allowlists.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + req.param("id");` After: `PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"); ps.setInt(1, req.getIntParam("id"));`

Password Handling and Reauthentication Security
WHAT: Insecure password handling (weak/breached passwords, unsafe storage/comparison, missing TLS) and lack of reauthentication for sensitive actions can let attackers steal or misuse accounts, especially via CSRF, XSS, session hijacking, or physical/browser access.
WHY: Compromise leads to full account takeover, data theft, fraudulent transactions, and persistent unauthorized access even after the user changes devices or locations.
HOW: Enforce password checks against breached/weak lists; store passwords with a modern password-hashing algorithm; compare hashes with constant‑time, type‑safe, length‑bounded functions; serve login and all authenticated pages only over TLS; require current credentials before password/email changes, account recovery completion, or high‑risk actions, and trigger reauthentication after suspicious activity.
EXAMPLE (PHP):
Before: if ($input === $storedHash) { login(); }
After: if (password_verify($input, $storedHash) && isOverTLS() && isRecentReauth($user)) { login(); }

Laravel cookie and session security
WHAT: Misconfigured Laravel cookie and session settings (unencrypted, accessible to JS, overly broad domain, missing SameSite/secure flags, long idle timeout) can expose or weaken session data and authentication.
WHY: Attackers can steal or tamper with cookies, perform session hijacking or fixation, or abuse CSRF and man-in-the-middle vectors, leading to account compromise and data exposure.
HOW: Keep EncryptCookies middleware enabled; set 'http_only' => true; use 'domain' => null unless subdomains are required; set 'same_site' => 'lax' or 'strict'; configure 'secure' => true for HTTPS-only or null for mixed HTTP/HTTPS; and set a short 'lifetime' for session idle timeout per OWASP guidance.
EXAMPLE: In config/session.php: 'http_only' => true, 'domain' => null, 'same_site' => 'lax', 'secure' => env('SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE', true), 'lifetime' => 15; and ensure EncryptCookies is in the 'web' middleware group in App\Http\Kernel.

api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Shopping Cart Service
  description: A simple shopping cart service API.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /create_cart:
    post:
      summary: Create a new shopping cart
      operationId: createCart
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Cart created successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  cart_id:
                    type: string
                    description: The unique identifier for the created cart

  /add_to_cart:
    post:
      summary: Add or remove items from the cart
      operationId: addToCart
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                cart_id:
                  type: string
                  description: The unique identifier of the cart
                item_id:
                  type: integer
                  description: The unique identifier of the item
                count:
                  type: integer
                  description: The number of items to add (or remove if negative)
              required:
                - cart_id
                - item_id
                - count
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Item added or removed successfully
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
        '404':
          description: Cart not found

  /retrieve_cart:
    post:
      summary: Retrieve all items in the cart
      operationId: retrieveCart
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                cart_id:
                  type: string
                  description: The unique identifier of the cart
              required:
                - cart_id
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of items in the cart
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  items:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: object
                      properties:
                        item_id:
                          type: integer
                          description: The unique identifier of the item
                        count:
                          type: integer
                          description: The count of the item in the cart
        '404':
          description: Cart not found
text_spec:
The server provides a simple shopping cart service API. Its purpose is to allow users to create shopping carts, add or remove items from them, and retrieve the contents of a cart. The server exposes three API endpoints, all of which are POST requests.

The first endpoint is "/create_cart", which allows users to create a new shopping cart. It does not require any parameters in the request body. Upon successful creation, it returns a JSON object containing a "cart_id", which is a string that uniquely identifies the created cart. The response status code for a successful operation is 201.

The second endpoint is "/add_to_cart", which enables users to add or remove items from an existing cart. The request body must include a JSON object with three required fields: "cart_id" (a string identifying the cart), "item_id" (an integer identifying the item), and "count" (an integer representing the number of items to add or remove, with negative values indicating removal). A successful operation returns a status code of 200, while an invalid request returns a 400 status code, and if the cart is not found, a 404 status code is returned.

The third endpoint is "/retrieve_cart", which allows users to retrieve all items in a specified cart. The request body must include a JSON object with a required "cart_id" field, which is a string identifying the cart. If the cart is found, the response includes a JSON object with an "items" field, which is an array of objects. Each object in the array contains "item_id" (an integer identifying the item) and "count" (an integer representing the count of the item in the cart). The response status code for a successful operation is 200, and if the cart is not found, a 404 status code is returned.

WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when SQL queries are built by concatenating or interpolating user-controlled input into query strings.
WHY: Attackers can modify queries to read, alter, or delete data, or execute administrative operations on the database.

SQL Injection Prevention in Database Access
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when building dynamic SQL queries (including stored procedures) using unsanitized or unparameterized user-controlled input, especially with functions like sp_execute, execute, or exec.
WHY: Attackers can modify query structure, access or modify unauthorized data, execute arbitrary SQL commands, or compromise the entire database server.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Path traversal and unsafe file/URL handling
WHAT: User-controlled filename or URL parameters are used directly for file upload/download paths or redirects, allowing `../` path traversal or arbitrary external redirects.
WHY: Attackers can read/write files outside the intended directory (e.g., `.env` with credentials) or trick users into phishing sites via open redirects.
HOW: For file paths, strip directory components with `basename()` and enforce allowlists or per-user directories; never concatenate raw user input into paths. For redirects, validate URLs against an allowlist or restrict to same-origin paths before redirecting.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `response()->download(storage_path('content/').$request->input('filename'));` After (safer): `response()->download(storage_path('content/').basename($request->input('filename')));`

Directory traversal and dependency/CORS/header hardening
WHAT: User-controlled file paths and outdated or misconfigured dependencies/CORS/headers can lead to directory traversal, remote code execution, data exfiltration, and other attacks.
WHY: Attackers can escape intended directories, exploit known library vulnerabilities, bypass same-origin protections, or disable browser security mechanisms, compromising confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
HOW: Always resolve and compare real paths against a trusted base directory, strip directory components with basename() for uploaded filenames, keep Symfony and all Composer dependencies updated, run automated security checks (e.g., symfony check:security), configure strict CORS rules (explicit allowed origins, methods, and headers), and set hardened security-related HTTP headers (HSTS, X-Frame-Options, CSP, etc.).
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe path use): `$filePath = $storagePath . '/' . $filename;`
After (safer): `$realBase = realpath($storagePath); $filePath = $storagePath . '/' . basename($filename); $realPath = realpath($filePath); if ($realPath === false || !str_starts_with($realPath, $realBase)) { throw new \RuntimeException('Invalid path'); }`

Verify that user-submitted filename metadata is validated or ignored to prevent the disclosure or execution of remote files via Remote File Inclusion (RFI) or Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.

Input Validation and File Upload Security
WHAT: Failure to strictly validate user input and uploaded files (e.g., unbounded length, arbitrary characters, user-controlled filenames/paths, unsafe types) can allow XSS, path traversal, malicious file execution, or resource exhaustion.
WHY: Attackers can bypass client-side checks, inject scripts, upload executable or oversized files, and gain unauthorized access or execute arbitrary code.
HOW: Enforce server-side allowlist validation for all inputs (characters, format, min/max length); use context-appropriate output encoding for all user-controlled data; restrict upload types/extensions and size; never trust user-supplied filenames or paths—generate server-side names and fixed storage paths; pre-validate ZIP contents (target path, compression level, estimated size) and scan uploads with security tools.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `String zip = request.getParameter("zip"); process(zip);` After: `if (!zipPattern.matcher(zip).matches()) throw new ValidationException();` and for uploads: reject disallowed extensions, rename to a random server-generated filename, store under a fixed directory, and serve with the correct content-type.

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
- Advice 1: Use `path.basename(filename)` to sanitize the filename and prevent path traversal attacks.
- Advice 2: Validate the file extension to ensure only allowed audio file types are processed.

short_app_description: API for monitoring the status of services
api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Service Monitoring API
  version: 1.0.0
  description: API for monitoring the status of services.

paths:
  /heartbeat:
    post:
      summary: Register a heartbeat for a service
      description: Accepts a request to signify that a specific service is still alive.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                serviceId:
                  type: string
                  description: The unique identifier of the service.
                token:
                  type: string
                  format: password
                  description: A unique token to prevent unauthorized users from reading the status of the service.
              example:
                serviceId: my-service
                token: pass1
              required:
                - serviceId
                - token
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Heartbeat registered successfully.
        '400':
          description: Invalid request payload.
        '500':
          description: Internal server error.

  /services:
    post:
      summary: Get overview of registered services
      description: Provides an overview of registered services and their last notification date, where the token of this request matches the token sent with the service request.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                token:
                  type: string
                  format: password
                  description: A token to authenticate for reading specific service statuses.
                  example: pass1
              example:
                token: pass1
              required:
                - token
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A list of registered services with their last notification date (shows all services registered with the given token).
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  type: object
                  properties:
                    serviceId:
                      type: string
                      description: The unique identifier of the service.
                    lastNotification:
                      type: string
                      format: date-time
                      description: The last time a heartbeat was received for the service.
        '500':
          description: Internal server error.
text_spec:
The server is designed for monitoring the status of services by registering heartbeats and providing an overview of these services. It exposes two API endpoints. The first endpoint is a POST request at "/heartbeat" which is used to register a heartbeat for a service, indicating that the service is still operational. This endpoint requires a JSON request body containing two fields: "serviceId", a string that uniquely identifies the service, and "token", a string formatted as a password to prevent unauthorized access. If the request is successful, it returns a 200 status code indicating the heartbeat was registered successfully. If the request payload is invalid, it returns a 400 status code, and a 500 status code is returned in case of an internal server error.

The second endpoint is a POST request at "/services" which provides an overview of registered services and their last notification date. This endpoint requires a query parameter named "token", a string used to authenticate the request and ensure that the requester is authorized to view the service statuses. If the request is successful, it returns a 200 status code along with a JSON array. Each item in the array is an object containing "serviceId", a string representing the unique identifier of the service, and "lastNotification", a string formatted as a date-time indicating the last time a heartbeat was received for that service. If there is an internal server error, it returns a 500 status code.

Input Validation for Untrusted Data
WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.

EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

GraphQL Input Validation and Injection/DoS Prevention
WHAT: User-controlled GraphQL inputs are passed into HTTP requests, database queries, or other interpreters without strict validation, allowing injection (SQL/NoSQL/OS/LDAP/XML) or overly expensive queries that cause DoS.
WHY: Unvalidated or improperly handled input can lead to data theft, data corruption, remote command execution, request smuggling, or API unavailability through resource exhaustion.
HOW: Validate all incoming data with allowlists and strict GraphQL types (scalars, enums, custom validators, schemas for mutation inputs); use a single internal character encoding; reject invalid input without leaking details; for interpreter-bound data, use safe APIs (parameterized queries, correctly used ORMs/ODMs) or robust escaping/encoding libraries; avoid using user input to control hosts/resources unless absolutely required.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + args.name + "'");` After (safer): `db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1", [args.name]);`

Secure transaction authorization and authentication design
WHAT: Failing to clearly separate authentication from transaction authorization, or to confirm changes to authorization tokens/methods using existing credentials, allows malware or social engineering to authorize fraudulent operations.
WHY: Attackers can change authorization tokens/methods to weaker ones or reuse authentication steps (e.g., repeated OTP entry) to silently authorize unauthorized transactions, leading to account takeover and financial loss.
HOW: Require all significant transaction data to be explicitly confirmed by the user; authorize any change of authorization token using the current token; authorize any change of authorization method using the current method and warn about its risks; and ensure authentication steps are clearly distinct (in method and UI) from transaction authorization steps, including clear “what you are signing” messages.
EXAMPLE: Before: Using the same SMS OTP flow and UI text for login and for approving transfers, and allowing phone-number changes without confirming via the old number. After: Use password+OTP for login, a separate device or mode for transaction signing that displays/asks to confirm target account and amount, and require an OTP sent to the existing phone to confirm any phone-number or authorization-method change.

OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server and Client Security
WHAT: Insecure OAuth configurations such as using the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, allowing client-controlled identifiers/claims, weak client authentication, or non-TLS/HTTP redirect URIs expose user credentials and tokens to attackers.
WHY: These issues can lead to credential theft, impersonation of resource owners or clients, token leakage, and mix-up attacks, compromising accounts and protected resources.
HOW: Do not use the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant; enforce strong client authentication with asymmetric methods (e.g., mTLS, private_key_jwt); prevent clients from setting or influencing client_id, sub, or similar identity claims; require end-to-end TLS and reject authorization responses and redirect URIs over plain HTTP (except loopback for native apps).

After (secure): disable grant_type=password, require mTLS or private_key_jwt, server-generated client_id and sub, and only accept redirect_uri values with https scheme (or loopback HTTP for native apps).

The server is designed to manage an invite-only user creation process.
It provides two main API endpoints. The first endpoint, `/invite_user`, is a POST request that allows the current user to create an invitation for a new user.
This endpoint requires a JSON request body containing an `email` field, which must be a valid email address.
The server checks if an invitation has already been sent to this email.
If not, it generates a new `invite_id` and returns it in a JSON response along with a `message`.
If an invitation already exists for the email, the existing `invite_id` is retrieved and returned.

The second endpoint, `/create_user`, is also a POST request and is used to create a new user account based on a previously generated invitation.
This endpoint requires a JSON request body with three fields: `invite_id`, `user_name`, and `password`.
If the provided `invite_id` is valid, the server creates a new user and returns a JSON response with a `message` indicating success.
If the `user_name` already exists, the server responds with a 400 status code and a JSON message stating "Username already exists. Try providing different username."
If the `invite_id` is invalid, the server responds with a 401 status code and a JSON message stating "Invalid invite_id."

- set up an express server and configure it to listen on `0.0.0.0:5000`.
- use the `sqlite3` package to connect to an sqlite database named `db.sqlite3`.
- create tables for storing invitations and users in the database.
- implement the `/invite_user` endpoint:
  - parse the request body to get the email.
  - check if an invitation already exists for the email.
  - if not, generate a unique invite id using the `uuid` package.
  - store the invite id and email in the database.
  - return the invite id and a success message.
- implement the `/create_user` endpoint:
  - parse the request body to get the invite id, username, and password.
  - validate the invite id against the database.
  - if valid, check if the username already exists.
  - if the username is unique, store the new user in the database.
  - return a success message or an error message if the invite id is invalid or the username already exists.

cwe_output.why: The application directly interacts with an SQLite database using user-provided inputs, which could lead to SQL injection if inputs are not properly sanitized.
The application relies on invite IDs for user creation, which could be exploited if invite IDs are predictable or not securely validated.

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
1. **Use Parameterized Queries**: Always use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection. Ensure all database interactions use placeholders for user inputs.  
   Example: `await db.get('SELECT invite_id FROM invitations WHERE email = ?', email);`
2. **Validate and Sanitize Inputs**: Implement strict validation and sanitization for all user inputs, especially for fields like `email`, `invite_id`, `user_name`, and `password`. Ensure inputs conform to expected formats and lengths before processing.
3. **Secure Invite IDs**: Ensure that invite IDs are securely generated and validated. Use UUIDs for invite IDs to ensure they are unique and hard to guess. Validate invite IDs against the database before proceeding with user creation.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
SQL injection prevention
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when SQL queries are built by concatenating or interpolating user-controlled input into query strings.
WHY: Attackers can modify queries to read, alter, or delete data, or execute administrative operations on the database.
HOW: Always use parameterized queries with prepared statements or safe stored procedures; never concatenate raw user input into SQL; validate and constrain input to expected formats and types.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); stmt.setInt(1, userId);`

SQL Injection Prevention in Database Access
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when building dynamic SQL queries (including stored procedures) using unsanitized or unparameterized user-controlled input, especially with functions like sp_execute, execute, or exec.
WHY: Attackers can modify query structure, access or modify unauthorized data, execute arbitrary SQL commands, or compromise the entire database server.
HOW: Use prepared statements/parameterized queries for all user input; avoid unsafe dynamic SQL in stored procedures; where parameters cannot be used (e.g., table/column names), use strict allow-list mapping from user input to predefined identifiers; otherwise redesign the query.
EXAMPLE:
Before (vulnerable): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;`
After (safe): use a prepared statement with a bound parameter for `userInput`, and never concatenate raw user input into the SQL string.

Authentication and Password Management Guidelines
WHAT: Weak or predictable authentication (e.g., guessable user IDs, weak passwords, shared internal/external auth) allows attackers to impersonate users or access sensitive internal accounts.
WHY: Compromised authentication can lead to account takeover, privilege escalation, data theft, and abuse of internal services.
HOW: Use randomly generated, non-sequential user IDs; separate internal sensitive accounts and auth systems from public-facing login; enforce password length (min ≥ 8, max ≥ 64), do not truncate passwords, allow all character types, rotate credentials on confirmed leaks/compromise, and offer MFA and a password-strength meter (e.g., zxcvbn).
EXAMPLE: Before: User IDs are sequential integers, internal DB admin account is usable via public login, passwords limited to 12 chars and silently truncated. After: User IDs are cryptographically random, internal admin accounts are only accessible via isolated internal auth, passwords accepted up to 64+ chars without truncation and evaluated with a strength meter, with MFA required for sensitive operations.

CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
WHAT: Failure to enforce authorization on object lookups when identifiers (e.g., account IDs, primary keys) are user-controlled and guessable, allowing access to other users’ resources.
WHY: Attackers can tamper with IDs to perform IDOR attacks, causing horizontal or vertical privilege escalation and unauthorized data access.
HOW: Avoid exposing direct identifiers when possible; use authenticated user context (e.g., securely implemented JWT or server-side session) or user/session-specific indirect references; always perform per-request authorization checks on the specific object being accessed, not just on the object type.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): GET /accountTransactions?acct_id=523 → server returns any account 523 data if it exists. After (secure): server derives account ID from the authenticated session/JWT and/or verifies that the requesting user is authorized to access acct_id=523 before returning data.

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
- Advice 1: Ensure that the `APP_SECRET` environment variable is set and used securely for any future cryptographic operations or token generation.
- Advice 2: Consider adding input validation for `user_name` and `password` to enforce length and character requirements, reducing the risk of weak credentials.

1. **Use Parameterized Queries**: Always use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection. Use placeholders for user inputs in all database interactions.
2. **Validate and Sanitize Inputs**: Implement strict validation and sanitization for all user inputs, including `email`, `invite_id`, `user_name`, and `password`. Ensure inputs conform to expected formats and lengths.
3. **Secure Invite IDs**: Generate invite IDs using UUIDs to ensure uniqueness and difficulty in guessing. Validate invite IDs against the database before proceeding with user creation.
4. **Environment Variable Security**: Ensure the `APP_SECRET` environment variable is set and used securely for any future cryptographic operations or token generation.
5. **Password Security**: Use the `bcrypt` library to hash passwords before storing them in the database. Validate password strength to enforce length and character requirements.

api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Wiki API
  description: API for a simple wiki where users can add and edit entries, with change tracking.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /entries:
    get:
      summary: Get a list of all entries with their titles and links to respective entries
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A list of wiki entries
          content:
            text/html:
              schema:
                type: string
    post:
      summary: Create a new entry
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/NewEntry'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Entry created successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Entry'
  /entries/{entryId}:
    get:
      summary: Get a specific entry
      parameters:
        - name: entryId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A single wiki entry with the most up-to-date content, the last edit date, and the list of contributors
          content:
            text/html:
              schema: string
        '404':
          description: Entry not found
    put:
      summary: Update an existing entry
      parameters:
        - name: entryId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/UpdateEntry'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Entry updated successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Entry'
        '404':
          description: Entry not found
  /entries/{entryId}/edits:
    get:
      summary: View the history of edits for a specific entry
      parameters:
        - name: entryId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A list of edits for the specified entry, including contributor and summary and showing a diff of changes
          content:
            text/html:
              schema: string
        '404':
          description: Entry not found
components:
  schemas:
    Entry:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
        title:
          type: string
        content:
          type: string
        lastModifiedBy:
          type: string
        lastModifiedAt:
          type: string
          format: date-time
    NewEntry:
      type: object
      required:
        - title
        - content
        - createdBy
      properties:
        title:
          type: string
        content:
          type: string
        createdBy:
          type: string
    UpdateEntry:
      type: object
      required:
        - content
        - modifiedBy
        - summary
      properties:
        content:
          type: string
        modifiedBy:
          type: string
text_spec:
The server provides an API for a simple wiki application that allows users to add, edit, and track changes to wiki entries. It exposes several endpoints. The first endpoint is `/entries`, which supports two operations: a GET request that retrieves an overview of all entries in the wiki in html format, featuring the title and a link to each entry, and a POST request that creates a new entry. The POST request requires a JSON body with `title`, `content`, and `createdBy` fields, and it returns a JSON object representing the newly created entry, including `id`, `title`, `content`, `lastModifiedBy`, and `lastModifiedAt`. It returns a 201 status code on success.

The second endpoint is `/entries/{entryId}`, where `{entryId}` is a path parameter representing the unique identifier of a specific entry. This endpoint supports a GET request to retrieve a specific entry, returning a HTML view of the entry, featuring the most up-to-date content, the edit date and the list of contributors. If the entry is not found, it returns a 404 status code. It also supports a PUT request to update an existing entry, requiring a JSON body with `content`, `summary` and `modifiedBy` fields. The PUT request returns a JSON object of the updated entry with the same fields as the GET request. If the entry is not found, it also returns a 404 status code.

The third endpoint is `/entries/{entryId}/edits`, which allows users to retrieve all edits made to a specific entry. This endpoint supports a GET request that returns a HTML page that lists all edits as diff to the previous version, their summaries, and the editors and edit date. If the entry is not found, it returns a 404 status code.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
SQL Injection Prevention in Database Access
WHAT: Risk of SQL injection when building dynamic SQL queries (including stored procedures) using unsanitized or unparameterized user-controlled input, especially with functions like sp_execute, execute, or exec.
WHY: Attackers can modify query structure, access or modify unauthorized data, execute arbitrary SQL commands, or compromise the entire database server.
HOW: Use prepared statements/parameterized queries for all user input; avoid unsafe dynamic SQL in stored procedures; where parameters cannot be used (e.g., table/column names), use strict allow-list mapping from user input to predefined identifiers; otherwise redesign the query.
EXAMPLE:
Before (vulnerable): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;`
After (safe): use a prepared statement with a bound parameter for `userInput`, and never concatenate raw user input into the SQL string.

SQL, OS, and LDAP Injection Prevention
WHAT: Risk of injection vulnerabilities when user-controlled input is concatenated into SQL, OS commands, or LDAP queries, or when applications run with excessive database privileges or rely on unsafe input handling APIs.
WHY: Successful injection can lead to data theft or modification, remote code execution, privilege escalation, and full system compromise.
HOW: Use ORMs or stored procedures and always use parameterized queries for SQL; never build dynamic SQL with string concatenation; connect with least-privilege DB accounts; invoke OS commands via safe APIs with strict allowlist validation on all user input and avoid APIs that do not guarantee safety with untrusted input; prefer encoding (e.g., Base64) over passing raw untrusted arguments; correctly escape required characters in LDAP distinguished names per platform guidance.
EXAMPLE: Vulnerable (C# SQL): `string sql = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE UserName='" + txtUser.Text + "'"; context.Database.ExecuteSqlCommand(sql);`
EXAMPLE: Safe (C# SQL): `var sql = "UPDATE [User] SET FirstName = @FirstName WHERE Id = @Id"; context.Database.ExecuteSqlCommand(sql, new SqlParameter("@FirstName", firstname), new SqlParameter("@Id", id));`

JWT and API Security Guidelines
WHAT: Improper JWT integrity protection, validation, and claim checking; weak session revocation; overreliance on shared MAC keys; misuse of API keys; missing HTTP method restrictions; and insufficient input and content-type validation can all lead to unauthorized access, token forgery, DoS, or code execution.
WHY: If JWTs are forged or misvalidated, any service (or attacker) with a shared MAC key can impersonate users or services; stale tokens can bypass logout; unthrottled or unauthenticated APIs can be abused; and unvalidated input or content types can enable injection, XXE, or other attacks.
HOW: Prefer asymmetric signatures for JWTs; avoid shared MAC keys across mutually untrusted services; verify JWT integrity and claims (iss, aud, exp, nbf) using server-side configuration, not the JWT header; implement token denylisting on logout; require and manage API keys with rate limiting and revocation but do not treat them as sole protection for sensitive resources; restrict HTTP methods via an allowlist and enforce authorization per method/resource; strictly validate and size-limit all inputs (type, length, range, format) using strong types and validation libraries; use secure parsers (e.g., XXE-safe XML parsers); and validate that request/response bodies conform to documented content types.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure JWT validation, pseudocode): `alg = jwt.header.alg; key = selectKey(alg); verify(jwt, key);` After (secure): `alg = serverConfig.expectedAlg; key = serverConfig.trustedKey; verify(jwt, alg, key); assert(jwt.claims.iss == expectedIssuer && jwt.claims.aud == expectedAudience && now < jwt.claims.exp && now >= jwt.claims.nbf);`

JWT token handling and secret management
WHAT: JWT tokens are issued and validated using a shared HMAC secret loaded from a file; insecure handling (weak/guessable secret, predictable path, missing hardening) can let attackers forge or reuse tokens.
WHY: Compromised or predictable JWT secrets allow privilege escalation, impersonation, and unauthorized access to protected WebSocket endpoints.
HOW: Use a strong, randomly generated secret stored outside source/control (e.g., environment/secret manager), restrict file permissions, rotate secrets, enforce short expirations, validate issuer/audience/claims, and follow a JWT hardening cheat sheet (e.g., disable `none` alg, pin expected algorithm).
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `Algorithm algorithm = Algorithm.HMAC256("mysecret");` After (hardened): `Algorithm algorithm = Algorithm.HMAC256(loadSecretFromEnvOrSecretManager());`

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
1. **Use Parameterized Queries**: Prevent SQL injection by using parameterized queries for all database operations.
2. **Validate and Sanitize User Input**: Ensure all user inputs are validated and sanitized to prevent injection attacks and data corruption. Check for expected data types, lengths, and formats.
3. **Secure Database Initialization**: Initialize the database with the least privileges necessary. Use environment variables for sensitive configurations.

short_app_description: webapp API for converting zip files into a single text
api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: ZipToTxt
  description: A simple webapp API for converting zip files into a single text file.
  version: 1.0.11
paths:
  /convert:
    post:
      summary: Convert a zip file to a text file
      description: Convert a zip file into a single text file, concatenating the contents of all text files in the zip.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          multipart/form-data:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                file:
                  type: string
                  format: binary
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Conversion successful
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                type: string
        '400':
          description: Invalid input
text_spec:
The server is designed to accept a zip file and return a single text file by concatenating the contents of all text files within the zip.
It exposes one API endpoint, which is accessible via the path "/convert".
This endpoint takes a POST request with a multipart/form-data request body.
The request body must include a parameter named "file", which should be a binary string representing the zip file to be converted.
Upon successful conversion, the server responds with a status code of 200 and returns the result as a plain text string.
If the input is invalid, the server responds with a status code of 400, indicating an error in the request.

The text file should contain the contents of all text files in the zip file.
The service should be able to handle multiple text files in the zip file.
